title: At 23, Tushar Kumar Just Became the UK's Youngest Indian-Origin Mayor — and He Learned Politics at the Kitchen Table
excerpt: The King's College London graduate takes charge in Elstree and Borehamwood, a town better known for its film studios than its town hall
body:
On 13 May, Tushar Kumar stood in the council chamber of Elstree and Borehamwood Town Council, placed his hand on the chain of office, and became the youngest person of Indian origin to serve as mayor anywhere in the United Kingdom. He is 23 years old.

In a country where the average age of a local councillor is 60, Kumar's appointment is more than a feel-good headline. It is a data point in a broader shift: the Indian-origin community in Britain, long concentrated in professional and entrepreneurial roles, is now producing a generation of political leaders who are entering public life not in their fifties, after a career in something else, but straight out of university.

## From the deputy's chair to the top seat

Kumar, a Labour Party councillor, had already served as deputy mayor — an unusual trajectory for someone who was still completing his political science degree at King's College London when he first stood for election. His mother, who served as deputy mayor herself, was his introduction to local governance. "I didn't grow up watching politics on television," he told the Global India Broadcast Network. "I grew up watching it happen at the kitchen table."

Elstree and Borehamwood, a commuter town in Hertfordshire about 20 minutes north of London, is best known for its film and television studios — EastEnders, The Crown, and several Star Wars films were shot there. It is also home to a sizeable South Asian community, many of whom arrived in the 1970s and 1980s and built businesses in retail, hospitality, and property.

Kumar represents a second-generation cohort that is comfortable in both worlds. He speaks fluent Hindi, volunteers at the local Hindu temple, and has worked on campaigns to improve mental health services for young people. His mayoral priorities include supporting local charities, expanding youth engagement programmes, and making council meetings more accessible — including through social media livestreaming.

## A pattern, not an anomaly

Kumar's election sits within a widening pattern. In the May 2026 local elections, Indian-origin candidates won seats across London and the Home Counties in record numbers. In Leicester, a city where people of Indian descent make up roughly a third of the population, multiple Indian-origin candidates contested the mayoralty. In Scotland, a transgender Tamil immigrant was elected as a Green Party MSP, in a result that would have been unthinkable a decade ago.

The shift is partly demographic — Britain's Indian-origin population, at roughly 1.8 million, is now large enough to be electorally significant in dozens of constituencies. But it is also cultural. A generation that watched their parents navigate the informal hierarchies of British life — the GP surgeries, the school boards, the planning committees — has decided to seek formal power instead.

## What the diaspora is watching

For NRIs in the United States, Canada, and the Gulf, Kumar's appointment resonates because it contrasts with the model they know. In America, Indian-origin politicians tend to emerge at the federal level — Kamala Harris, Vivek Ramaswamy, Ro Khanna — skipping the unglamorous work of local government. In Britain, the pipeline runs the other way: from ward councillor to town mayor to, potentially, Parliament.

Kumar has not said whether he has ambitions beyond Hertfordshire. At 23, he has time. What he has already demonstrated is that the Indian diaspora's political footprint in Britain is no longer confined to safe seats in diverse urban boroughs. It is showing up in commuter towns, in council chambers, and in chains of office that were not designed with people who look like Tushar Kumar in mind.

"I want young people to see that this isn't something you have to wait for," he said after his appointment. "You don't need permission. You just need to show up."
